name: Nikhil Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at a distribution centre for a DIY chain, the one by the motorway junction. I came in through an agency eight months ago and I'm still agency, rolling on from week to week. It's heavy stuff: boxes of floor tiles, paint tins, bags of grout, the odd toilet. I pick to a trolley, wrap the pallet and push it to the loading bay.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out most, and what keeps you there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The weight wears me out, and the not knowing. The agency texts the shifts on a Sunday night, so some weeks I get five days and some weeks three. What I like is that it's simple, you pick it, you wrap it, you're done. And there's a few of us who go for chips after the Friday shift, which is about the only treat I get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, that's that then. I'm not one for big opinions online, I'd probably not say anything. At work maybe a joke about how the scanners are still rubbish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, AI was never my problem. My problem is being agency and short of money. Nothing about this changes that, so I'm in the same spot I was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Turn up every shift they offer, keep my head down, and try to get my pick rate up so they make me permanent. If I get permanent, I'd start putting something aside, even 25 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as always, which isn't great. A low hum of worry, like a fridge you stop noticing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the Sunday texts. What happens in a three-day week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lucy, my partner, covers more of the rent that week and I feel rubbish about it. She's a hairdresser, so her money goes up and down too. A three-day week means we skip the food shop top-up and live on what's in the freezer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has anyone said when you might go permanent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The supervisor, Gary, said 'maybe after Christmas'. He said that last Christmas too, to someone else. I'm not counting on it, but I'm not leaving either, there's nothing else round here that's better.

say: **Fair enough**, that's that; I'm not one for big opinions online.
I might joke at work that the **scanners** are still rubbish.
think: AI was never my problem; being **agency** and **short of money** is.
Nothing here changes that, so I'm in the **same spot** as before.
do: Turn up for every **shift offered** and keep my head down.
Push my **pick rate** up to get a permanent contract.
Save **25 a month** if I go permanent.
feel: A **low hum of worry**, like a fridge you stop noticing.
S0.quote: AI was never my problem. My problem is being agency and short of money.
fieldNote: His worry is **agency insecurity**: shifts swing between three and five days a week.
He's quiet and **pragmatic**, with no one to blame, just a wish for stability.
Few better jobs nearby keep him **staying put**, waiting on a vague permanent offer.

steps.text: Take every agency shift offered and raise his pick rate
Put 25 a month aside if he gets a permanent contract

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. I'll read it as written. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was coming, wasn't it. Some jobs go, some come, that's how it's always been. I wouldn't be ranting about it, there's no point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It worries me more than I'd say. The office side would get leaner, and I reckon the first thing a leaner company does is cut the agency lot. Robots in our aisles are a bit further off, because the stuff is so heavy and awkward, but they'd come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as normal for a while and see what happens to the agency numbers. I'd stop the Friday chips and cancel the football channel, to keep a bit back. I wouldn't do a course or anything yet, not until I knew what the course was for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in my gut. Like when the boss walks the floor with a clipboard and doesn't say why.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the agency might get cut first. Why do you think that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's cheaper. Agency is the tap they can turn off without paperwork. When the planning computer says fewer bodies, it'll be the people with no contract who go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Lucy say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say do something, Nik. She always says that. And I'd say I am doing something, I'm turning up, which annoys her.

say: It was always coming; **some jobs go**, some come.
I wouldn't **rant** about it, because there's no point.
think: A leaner company cuts the **agency workers** first, and that's me.
Robots in our aisles are **further off**, because the stock is heavy and awkward.
do: Keep working as normal and **watch the agency numbers**.
Stop the **Friday chips** and cancel the football channel.
Hold off on any **course** until I know what it's for.
feel: **Uneasy in my gut**, like a boss with a clipboard who won't say why.
S1.quote: Agency is the tap they can turn off without paperwork.
fieldNote: He predicts **agency cuts** from leaner planning, a concrete fear behind a calm surface.
His idea of action is **turning up**, which frustrates his partner Lucy.
He won't **retrain** without knowing what the training leads to.

steps.text: Watch how many agency workers keep their shifts
Stop Friday chips and cancel the football channel
Keep turning up for every DIY warehouse shift offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. I'll read it as written. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, that's a lot, isn't it. People would be arguing online about whether it's good or bad, and I'd stay out of it. I'd just ask the lads what they're doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be finished in warehousing. I can't do much else, I left school early and I'm not quick with new tech. I'd have maybe three years of picking left, and agency means they could drop me sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything I could straight away, and stop going out. I'd look at getting my van licence, because people will still want someone to carry a toilet up the stairs for a few years. And if it got really bad, Lucy and I would move in with her mum, who has a spare room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My chest goes tight thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So the office side changes in 2028 but the robots come around 2031. What do those three years look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More pressure, fewer shifts and nobody explaining anything. The robots aren't in yet but everybody knows they're coming, so nobody's getting made permanent. I'd hang on and take any shift going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the agency dropped you in 2029?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panic, then go to the job centre, I suppose. I've never been, and I'd be embarrassed. Lucy's mum would help, but I hate the idea.

say: **That's a lot**, and I'd stay out of the online arguments.
I'd just ask the **lads at work** what they're planning to do.
think: I'd be **finished in warehousing** with no diploma and slow with tech.
Agency means they could **drop me** before the robots even arrive.
do: Cut **all spending** straight away and stop going out.
Get a **van licence** for delivery work carrying heavy goods.
Move in with **Lucy's mum** if things get bad.
feel: **Alarmed**, with a tight chest thinking about it.
S2.quote: I'd have maybe three years of picking left, and agency means they could drop me sooner.
fieldNote: He sees the robot gap as three years of **frozen hiring**, not a chance to plan.
His fallback is **family**, Lucy's mum, which he finds embarrassing.
He would visit a **job centre** for the first time, a sign of real alarm.

steps.text: Cut all non-essential spending and stop going out
Get a van licence to deliver heavy DIY goods
Move into Lucy's mum's spare room if money runs out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. I'll read it as written. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, I'd keep it to myself mostly, because talking about robots at work just winds people up. Maybe I'd tell the younger agency lads not to count on warehousing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for AGI, eight for robots, so I'd probably get made permanent and have a few years. But I'd still be someone with nothing else, and at 35 that's harder than at 27.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job and wait a couple of years to see how fast it really goes. Then I'd do the van licence once I had some money saved. I'd try to put 30 a month aside once I'm permanent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, slower. It's the same tight chest, it just comes later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. Would you start the van licence now or wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wait, probably. It costs money I haven't got, and I'd want to see whether vans are going the same way first. Lucy would hate that answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the warehouse you'd miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The simple bit. Pick it, wrap it, done. I don't know many jobs like that.

say: I'd **keep it to myself** mostly, because talking about robots at work just winds people up.
I'd tell the younger agency lads **not to count** on warehousing.
think: I'd probably go **permanent** and have a few years before robots.
At **35** I'd still have nothing else, which is harder than at 27.
do: Keep the job and **wait two years** to see how fast it moves.
Take a **van licence** once there's money saved.
feel: **Worried**, with the same tight chest arriving later.
S3.quote: I'd still be someone with nothing else, and at 35 that's harder than at 27.
fieldNote: More time leads him to **wait**, not plan; he delays even the cheap van licence.
He still expects to **lose the job** and has no real fallback.
He values the **simplicity** of picking, which few other jobs offer.

steps.text: Wait two years to see how fast warehouse robots spread
Save 30 a month once made permanent
Take a van licence once there's money saved

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. I'll read it as written. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, I'd worry about it in nine. That's what I'd say down the pub anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's still the end of my kind of work, it's just far off. I'd be 39 or 40 when robots can do the heavy picking. That's a long way away, and I'm bad at planning that far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do what I'm doing: stay, try to go permanent, keep my head down. Maybe in five years I'd think about a trade. I'm not going to pretend I'd start a course next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better. Still that low hum, but quieter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Does that make you want to plan, or put it off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Put it off, honestly. I know that's not the right answer. Lucy says I'm like this with the dentist too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you actually move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing a robot actually pick a box of tiles would make me move. Until then the whole robot thing is just talk to me.

say: Ten years is long; I'd worry about it **in nine**.
That's what I'd say **down the pub**, anyway.
think: It's still **the end** of my kind of work, just far off.
I'd be **39 or 40** when robots do the heavy picking.
do: Stay put, aim for a **permanent contract**, and keep my head down.
Consider a **trade** in about five years, not before.
feel: **Better**, with the low hum of worry turned down.
S4.quote: Seeing a robot actually pick a box of tiles would make me move. Until then the whole robot thing is just talk to me.
fieldNote: He openly **puts things off**, comparing it to avoiding the dentist.
His **agency status** and thin cushion keep him anxious even with a decade.
Only **seeing a robot** do his job would get him to act.

steps.text: Stay at the DIY warehouse and aim for a permanent contract
Wait until robots handle tiles before considering a trade

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'm agency, I've got nothing saved and nothing else I'm trained for. What would help is a proper contract, so I'm not the first out, and somebody telling me which training actually leads to a job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the agency side. People talk about workers like we're all on contracts. Half our floor isn't.

headlineQuote: People talk about workers like we're all on contracts. Half our floor isn't.
portrait: Nikhil is a **27-year-old agency picker** at a DIY warehouse, lifting tiles and paint, eight months in.
His shifts swing between **three and five days**, and his partner Lucy, a hairdresser, covers the gaps.
He's **pragmatic and quiet**, blames no one, and prefers turning up to planning.
He **puts off** change, waiting to see robots before acting, even with ten years' notice.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because as an agency worker with no savings he'd go first.
whatWouldHelp: A **permanent contract**, so he isn't first out.
Clear advice on which **training** actually leads to a job.
